summary:
SoilSense is a multilingual, WCAG 2.1 AA-compliant decision-support web app, paired with a phone line, that turns NASA climate observations and local soil data into tailored 3-year crop-rotation strategies for farmers. Shifting temperatures, erratic rainfall, and declining soil health make rotation choices risky, since a crop that builds soil in one field may exhaust water or miss frost windows in another.

SoilSense pulls 35 years of NASA POWER daily weather, filters for real climate trends with the Mann-Kendall test, and combines them with USDA SSURGO soil profiles and CDL crop history. It then simulates hundreds of rotations of corn, soybean, wheat, oats, alfalfa, and sorghum, with or without cover crops. The top three are ranked by the farmer’s goal (profit, soil health, lower risk, or balanced) and compared against “change nothing.” Every explanation is built from the data, not generated by AI. Across 43 crop–location series covering 13 counties, modeled yield variation was positively correlated with observed yields in 42 series, with an average correlation of 0.41..

Farmers can pick a field on a NASA satellite map or call in with no app or internet, and both channels use the same deterministic planning engine. By offering transparent trade-offs, zero login, and multilingual access, SoilSense puts a crop advisor in every farmer’s pocket, supporting local expertise rather than replacing it.
details:
https://github.com/jzeng151/soilsense

Overview

SoilSense is a web dashboard and phone line powered by a single engine. Farmers can call in, in their own language, share a zip code and their current crop, and hear a plain-language recommendation for what to plant next, with no app or internet required. Alternatively, they can select a field on a NASA satellite map in the dashboard and receive the same answer. The dashboard is entirely optional.

The recommendations target two compounding problems: climate change and continuous cropping, both of which erode yields and reduce biodiversity. SoilSense is designed to inform a farmer’s judgment, not replace it. It treats farmers as the experts on their own land and leaves every decision in their hands.

How it works

Under the hood, 35 years of NASA POWER daily weather (1991-2025) and 1 km Daymet data are filtered with a Mann-Kendall test, so only genuine climate trends remain. These are combined with USDA SSURGO soil properties (water-holding capacity, drainage, and texture) and CDL satellite-classified crop history. The model then simulates hundreds of 3-year rotations of corn, soybean, wheat, oats, alfalfa, and sorghum, with and without cover crops. Each season is scored on water and heat factors and combined into a rotation score, while a logistic regression predicts drought and weights drought years differently from normal ones. The top three are ranked by the farmer’s goal—profit, soil health, lower risk, or balanced—and compared against “change nothing.” Farmers can refine the comparison with their own soil tests, harvest records, crop requirements, and prices, making local knowledge part of the calculation. Farmers can go beyond choosing a priority: they can exclude unsuitable crops, require a crop in the rotation, and specify equipment and market constraints. Optional soil tests replace relevant mapped assumptions, while harvest records provide bounded local yield calibration. Farmers can also enter their own crop prices and explore how historical price variation affects the comparison. The hourly Field Watch function checks demo farms every hour, even when no one has the page open, for unusually dry rainfall and root-zone soil conditions using the latest available NASA daily observations.

We validated the results against independent sources. The Kansas model correlated with USDA county harvests at 0.51-0.72 (p < 0.001), and in 13 counties it had never seen, it correctly identified good and bad harvest years in 42 of 43 cases. OpenET satellite evapotranspiration checks the water model, USDA RMA crop-insurance loss records explain why bad years failed, and independent K-State research rotations offer a second opinion. Deterministic code calculates and ranks rotations; optional AI explanations and chat help farmers interpret the results.

Impact and creativity

SoilSense helps farmers improve yields in a way that is simple and respects their expertise. The intended impact is more resilient, productive, and biodiverse farms, shaped by farmers’ own decisions.

What sets it apart is who it is built for. NASA’s climate observations are usually locked inside dense GIS tools made for researchers and enterprise agribusiness. SoilSense puts them in the hands of farmers who rarely get to use them, as “a crop advisor in every farmer’s pocket,” reachable with a single phone call. Because both channels run on one engine, a farmer without internet gets the same answer as one on the dashboard. Trade-offs are transparent, and every reason traces back to the underlying data, so the advice can be checked.

Tools and design considerations

The project is built with TypeScript and React, deployed and served globally on Cloudflare Workers with a D1 cache. Twilio powers the phone calls, the Gemini API lets farmers chat for results, optional accounts use application-managed authentication, and GoDaddy provides the domain. Beyond the datasets above, we used NASA GIBS (MODIS) imagery for field selection and USDA NASS county yields and prices as ground truth. We also used Gemini, Claude, and GitHub Copilot for UI scaffolding, WCAG contrast and translation QA, data-parsing scripts, debugging, the crop-rotation model, analysis code, and research analysis.

The design was shaped by ease of use, language access, and respect for farmers’ expertise. The web interface supports English, Spanish, and Korean, with Korean currently AI-translated and awaiting native-speaker review. Selected English and Spanish planning flows have passed automated WCAG A/AA checks and keyboard tests; full accessibility conformance and screen-reader testing remain outstanding. Farmers can get a plan without creating an account, compare priorities rather than accept a single “best” answer, and bring their own measurements and practical constraints into the decision.
